generatedProse.concept-context: The School of Sport leans heavily on Kolb's Experiential Learning Cycle because so much of the field is learned by doing: running a training session, delivering a rehab programme, managing an event. The cycle insists you move past what happened and how it felt to abstract conceptualisation, connecting the experience to theory, evidence or professional guidance, before planning what to change. For a coach, a therapist or a sport scientist, that conceptualisation stage is where an anecdote about a session becomes genuine professional learning.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two sport coaching students reflect on the same training session that went badly when a new passing drill fell apart and the players disengaged.

Tom stops after the first two stages of the cycle. He describes the drill breaking down and the players losing focus, and observes that he felt flustered and that the group was noisy. The account is accurate, but it ends at observation: no concept is brought in to explain it, and no plan follows. It is a description with feelings attached.

Amara carries the same session through all four stages. After describing and observing, she reaches abstract conceptualisation: drawing on what she knows about task design and cognitive load, she sees that the drill demanded too much at once for the players' stage of learning. Then active experimentation: next time she will break the drill into progressions and set one clear constraint at a time. Her plan becomes the start of the next cycle.

Both began from the same session. Only Amara used the whole cycle, turning an event into a concept-led plan rather than a retelling.
generatedProse.summary: Across the School of Sport, Kolb's cycle turns an experience such as a training session, a test or a rehab appointment into learning by carrying it through concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualisation and active experimentation. Used critically, it forces the step from describing what happened to explaining it with concepts and planning what to change. You can now structure a reflection with the cycle, tell critical reflection from description, and reach a reasoned plan. The next lesson turns this into writing.

check.body: In the worked example, what made Amara's reflection critical rather than descriptive?

items.text: She explained the drill breaking down using concepts such as task design and cognitive load, and reached a concrete plan.
She described the drill and the players' noise in more vivid detail.
She spent longer describing how flustered she felt.
She identified which player was most at fault.

feedback.correct: That's right. Explaining the experience with coaching concepts and reaching a plan is what makes the reflection critical.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for the stages of the cycle that Tom left out.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara's reflection was critical because she conceptualised the session with coaching ideas and reached a plan, not because her description was more vivid or her feeling stronger.
